content: The Guidance on Regulations for the Transport of Infectious Substances 2019–2020, effective from January 1, 2019, was published by the World Health Organization (WHO) to provide comprehensive instructions on the safe handling and transportation of infectious substances. The WHO permits the reproduction, redistribution, and adaptation of this guidance for non-commercial purposes, provided proper citation is given. However, the use of the WHO logo is prohibited, and any adaptations must be licensed under equivalent Creative Commons terms. Translations of the document must include a disclaimer stating that WHO is not responsible for the accuracy or content of the translation, and the original English version remains the authoritative source. The document highlights the critical role of biological agents in detecting and preventing outbreaks of emerging and highly infectious diseases. Facilities handling such agents are responsible for their identification, secure storage, and containment in compliance with best practices. One of the most widely recognized frameworks for transporting dangerous goods, including infectious substances, is the UN Model Regulations on the Transport of Dangerous Goods. These recommendations, developed by the United Nations Committee of Experts on the Transport of Dangerous Goods (UNCETDG), are continuously updated every two years to reflect technical advancements, new materials, and emerging safety requirements. The UN Model Regulations provide a standardized set of provisions to harmonize national and international regulations while allowing flexibility for local adaptations. Specific international agreements govern the transport of dangerous goods by different modes of transport: 1. Air Transport: The International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) publishes the Technical Instructions for the Safe Transport of Dangerous Goods by Air, which are legally binding for all international flights. The International Air Transport Association (IATA) also issues Dangerous Goods Regulations (DGR), incorporating ICAO provisions and additional operational restrictions. 2. Rail Transport: The Regulations Concerning the International Carriage of Dangerous Goods by Rail (RID) apply to countries in Europe, the Middle East, and North Africa, as well as domestic transport within the European Union. 3. Road Transport: The European Agreement Concerning the International Carriage of Dangerous Goods by Road (ADR) applies to 49 countries and is also used in modified forms in South America and Southeast Asia. 4. Sea Transport: The International Maritime Organization (IMO) publishes the International Maritime Dangerous Goods Code, which is mandatory for all contracting parties to the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea (SOLAS). 5. Postal Services: The Universal Postal Union (UPU) aligns its Letter Post Manual with the UN Model Regulations, although high-risk infectious substances (Category A) are generally not accepted for postal shipment. National regulations often adopt the UN Model Regulations entirely or with variations to suit local conditions. In cases where multiple regulations apply to a single shipment, the most stringent requirements should be followed. Operators and carriers may impose additional safety requirements, which, while not legally binding, must be adhered to avoid service refusals or delays. Supplementary regulations may also apply, such as import/export licensing, agricultural safety, or environmental protection laws. Training is a critical component of the safe transport of infectious substances. All personnel involved in the preparation and handling of dangerous goods must receive appropriate training tailored to their specific roles and responsibilities. This includes general awareness, safety training, and function-specific training. Competency must be verified through testing, and training records should be maintained and made available for verification. Retraining is typically required every two years or as stipulated by national authorities. The document also provides detailed definitions and classifications of infectious substances, including cultures, patient specimens, medical waste, and contaminated medical devices. It outlines the specific requirements for transporting live animals infected with biological agents and the exemptions for non-pathogenic or inactivated materials. Genetically modified organisms (GMOs) and microorganisms (GMMOs) are classified as infectious substances if they can cause disease in humans or animals. In summary, the WHO guidance serves as a vital resource for ensuring the safe and compliant transport of infectious substances, protecting public health, and maintaining international health security.
